newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Fast M2 growth fuels Mauritius inflation-cen bank.
newsitem.headline: Fast M2 growth fuels Mauritius inflation-cen bank.

text.p: The central Bank of Mauritius said on Friday inflation was a major concern and its policy would in future focus on price stability.

"Although some progress has been made in containing the inflation rate, inflationary pressures still loom in our economy due to our recent experience of consumption driven growth," the central bank said in its 1995/96 annual report.
"A relatively tight monetary policy stance would need to be adopted in order to maintain the growth of liquidity at desirable levels," the central bank said.
"Price stability and a stable exchange rate of the rupee will constitute the basic objectives of the policy stance of the Bank of Mauritius."
Inflation in Mauritius is forecast at 6.5 percent in calendar 1996, up from 6.0 percent in 1995.

In his report, Bank Governor Dan Maraye said proceeds from $150 million of Floating Rate Notes (FRN) which Mauritius raised from the Eurobond market in October 1995 exacerbated the problem of excess liquidity in the monetary system.
"Monetary expansion continued to remain a major concern over the year...The growth rate of money supply, M2, shot up to 38.4 percent on annualised basis," Maraye said.
"Policy efforts were consistently directed towards containing inflation pressures in the economy," Maraye added.

To mop up excess liquidity, the government sold 296.4 million rupees of four year Independence Bonds and 2.079 billion rupees of five year Republic Bonds during the past financial year, the central bank report said.

In the financial year ending 30 June 1996, the central bank received bids totalling 26.352 billion rupees for the 53 weekly treasury bill auctions it held during the year, well above the 21.560 billion rupees of bills it put on tender.

"As banks were very liquid, they quoted prices while bidding at the primary auctions resulting in a general drop in yields," the report said. "The total amount of bids accepted for 1995/96 was of 18.205 billion rupees, accounting for 84.4 percent of the tender amount and 69.1 percent of the value of bids received."
In 1994/95, the central bank put on tender a total of 19.675 billion rupees of treasury bills in 53 weekly auctions and received bids totalling 13.798 billion rupees.
"For the year as a whole, the overall wieghted yield rate declined from 10.86 percent in 1994/95 to 9.63 percent for the year 1995/96, reflecting the excess demand for bills," the report said.
